reason: The sources provide over ten cross-verified claims across independent domain sources to support a compelling 45-second story about BepiColombo's trajectory, engineering challenges, and orbital capture.
story: To reach Mercury, falling into the Sun's deep gravity well requires more energy than sending a probe to Pluto. In October 2018, ESA and JAXA launched BepiColombo, a joint mission carrying two science orbiters—ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter and JAXA's Mio—stacked atop the ion-propelled Mercury Transfer Module. Named after Giuseppe 'Bepi' Colombo, the pioneer of planetary gravity assists, the spacecraft undertook a seven-year voyage executing nine planetary flybys past Earth, Venus, and Mercury to brake against solar gravity. Despite a cruise power anomaly that delayed arrival by a year, and a fourth Mercury flyby skimming just 165 kilometers above the surface, BepiColombo reached Mercury in November 2026. During insertion, a software glitch cut the main engine burn short, yet gravity still safely captured the probe, making it only the second mission ever to orbit the innermost planet.
angle: Placing a spacecraft into orbit around Mercury requires more energy than sending a mission all the way to Pluto because of the Sun's immense gravitational pull.

claims.claim: BepiColombo is a joint planetary exploration mission between the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA).
The mission is named in honor of Italian mathematician and engineer Giuseppe 'Bepi' Colombo.
Giuseppe Colombo calculated the interplanetary gravity assist maneuver used by NASA's Mariner 10 mission to fly past Mercury multiple times.
BepiColombo launched on October 20, 2018, aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from Europe's Spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana.
BepiColombo is only the second spacecraft mission in history to enter orbit around Mercury, following NASA's MESSENGER.
The mission includes two primary science orbiters: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio).
During its cruise phase, the spacecraft stack relied on the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) for electrical power and solar electric propulsion.
BepiColombo's flight plan required nine planetary gravity-assist flybys: one of Earth, two of Venus, and six of Mercury.
A power-related anomaly affecting the solar electric propulsion system delayed BepiColombo's final arrival at Mercury by roughly eleven months to a year.
During its fourth flyby of Mercury in September 2024, BepiColombo passed within 165 kilometers of the planet's surface.
BepiColombo achieved orbital capture around Mercury in November 2026.
A software glitch prematurely cut short the orbital insertion thruster burn, but the spacecraft was still captured into a stable orbit around Mercury.
The two scientific orbiters are scheduled to separate from each other in December following orbital entry.
JAXA's Mio orbiter was protected from intense solar radiation during cruise by ESA's Magnetospheric Orbiter Sunshield and Interface (MOSIF).
Mercury contains water ice located inside craters near its poles that remain in permanent shadow.

disputed: S6 mentions an early planned launch date of 2013 on a Soyuz-Fregat rocket, whereas later sources confirm it launched in 2018 on an Ariane 5; script should use the actual 2018 Ariane 5 launch.
S1 mentions potential detection of phosphine in Venus's atmosphere during flybys was disputed by follow-up studies; script should leave out phosphine or present it as unconfirmed/disputed.
